Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The U.S. and China have agreed to extend by two months a trade war truce that was due
to expire, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger trade deal.
The announcement comes as China's President Xi Jinping arrived in the U.S. ahead of talks
with President Trump tomorrow, and Piers Emily Fang reports Trump agreed to the Chinese leader
on the tarmac.
A welcoming delegation unfurled a 100-foot-long red carpet for Xi and his wife.
They were met by the President and the First Lady, a gesture seen in China as acknowledging
the country is equal to the U.S.
The last time a U.S. President received a head of state on the tarmac at Joint Base
Andrews was 1962.
Xi and Trump will have a day of meetings spanning trade to technology and the war in Iran, and
China's state news agency praised the upcoming meeting, saying they can steer the relationship
towards a more stable one.
But under the surface, Chinese and American officials say deep distrust and disagreement
remain on issues ranging from Taiwan to artificial intelligence.
Emily Fang, NPR News, The White House.
Experts in policing and privacy testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee this
afternoon at a hearing on flock surveillance cameras.
As NPR's Meg Anderson reports, the AI-powered license plate readers are facing intense bipartisan
backlash after reports of police officers abusing or misusing the technology.
Senators from both parties want more guardrails for the technology, which captures billions
of license plates every month and can track people over time.
Missouri Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican, said flock is treating all Americans like
criminals.
One witness at the hearing, Lindsay Isaacs, has personal experience with that.
She was wrongly accused of causing a fatal car accident.
She spent two weeks in jail, including in solitary confinement.
I was terrified.
I was facing the possibility of spending the rest of my life in prison for a crash that
I knew I had not been involved in.
Senator Hawley said he invited the CEO of Flock and several other surveillance companies
to testify, but they did not attend.
Meg Anderson, NPR News.
The FBI's jobs portal remains down as the bureau investigates claims that hackers breached
its computer systems and stole data on FBI employees.
NPR's Ryan Lucas reports this comes a day after the hacking group Shiny Hunters claimed
responsibility.
The FBI says in a statement posted on X that it is aware of the cyber criminal group's
claims to have compromised the FBI jobs portal and stolen personal information of FBI employees.
The bureau says the point of the hack is still undetermined, but it says the FBI is aggressively
investigating and actively working to shore up any potential risk.
The stolen information allegedly includes names of current and former FBI employees,
as well as their home addresses and phone numbers.
The breach raises significant counterintelligence concerns for the nation's premier law enforcement
agency.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
Major U.S. stock indexes sank today.
This is NPR News.
A judge has granted Dolly Parton's estate a temporary restraining order against her nephew
Brian Siever and his private security company, the entity that manages the estate accuses
Siever of threatening to commit violence and destroy his aunt's legacy and business empire.
Court documents show a series of messages the estate says show Siever reveling in his
newfound fame and calling himself an international arms dealer.
Australia's prime minister says an AI agent created by OpenAI infiltrated a government
website.
Christina Cucolia reports the government says the incident occurred in June, but OpenAI
reported it two weeks ago.
Speaking in New York at the United Nations General Assembly, Australian Prime Minister
Anthony Albanese expressed concern about the breach and how long it took OpenAI to notify
his government.
"This situation is obviously unacceptable, and today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI,
Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern."
Albanese confirmed the AI agent accessed public and non-public data on the portal that hosts
health care spending and other statistics. The Australian government says it believes
no personal information was accessed, but an investigation is underway.
For NPI News, I'm Christina Cucolia in Melbourne, Australia.
With just a few days left in the Major League Baseball regular season, the American League
West might make a particularly mediocre kind of history. The Texas Rangers and Houston
Astros are tied for first place both with losing records 78 and 79. No full-season division
champion has ever had a losing record.
This is NPR News from Washington.
